scores.why: A provides concrete Cedar Prairie templates, blocks and authoring deliverables, B gives a credible build plan without specifying those authoring assets, C also leaves the mandatory Akamai route unresolved, and D offers mostly architectural assertions with unclear deployment boundaries and little accountable build scope.

D best addresses the full page and PDF inventory, Compliance-controlled filing retention and URL testing, A covers documents and migration checks but offers weaker retirement criteria, B largely leaves document handling implicit, and C supplies generic migration mechanics without comparable retirement decisions or delivery commitments.

C adds enforceable automated checks, manual release testing and PDF triage but excludes PDF tagging, A and D provide equivalent substantive WCAG 2.2 testing plans with less explicit release enforcement and document coverage, and B does not address accessibility.

C and D equally combine explicit field Core Web Vitals thresholds, baselines and release controls, B offers useful Akamai and third-party script testing but relies on an inflexible Lighthouse 100 commitment without explicit field thresholds, and A provides little beyond the performance aspiration.

C directly specifies Akamai routing, cache rules, publishing purges, named security headers and validation, A and B equally explain origin-controlled caching and invalidation but leave security headers unspecified, and D omits the requested configuration details while treating the mandatory CDN choice as open.

D supplies the clearest permission-based approval gate, group routing and retained audit history, A provides useful Workfront review design with its separate license disclosed but does not establish how approval technically gates publishing, B includes a useful native workflow amid distracting prerequisites, and C substitutes general governance for a demonstrated Compliance publishing gate.

B and C offer substantially equivalent experiment plans, variant tracking and stopping discipline, D earns comparable credit through a tailored Akamai allocation design with Compliance approval and per-test commitments despite unresolved implementation details, and A never describes A/B testing.

B gives the strongest migration-specific freeze, full-URL checks and defined hypercare although rollback execution remains thin, A provides a basic launch and follow-up plan, D adds owned testing deliverables but leaves SEO and rollback mechanics weak, and C spends substantial space on generic architecture and deployment checks whose relevance to Edge Delivery is unclear.

A connects a tailored prompt portfolio to configured monitoring, answer inspection and a defined baseline report, D explains relevant visibility measures and sampling limits but concentrates implementation on traffic data, B stops largely at strategy, and C measures agent traffic and referrals rather than how assistants describe Cedar Prairie.

D most fully covers approved on-site improvements and third-party source work through quantified services, pitch assets and outreach records, A and B offer identical useful on-site content routines without off-site work, and C adds a quantified content cadence but likewise omits the third-party program.

C explicitly designs auto, home and life comparisons leading to the appropriate quote-start pages with source refresh and defined implementation effort, while A, B and D provide similarly useful sourcing, guardrail and staged-launch approaches but leave the requested comparison and quote journeys largely unspecified.

B specifically excludes superseded filings, rate quotes and claim decisions and supplies a Compliance-approved source register and regression tests, A directly explains grounding, refresh and refusal behavior but lacks comparable client-specific controls, and C and D equally offer generic guardrails and testing without defining the regulated boundaries.

C directly commits to a Genesys queue bridge, context mapping, after-hours handling and agent pilot with disclosed licensing and effort although integration feasibility remains unproven, A and B describe only generic handoffs without Genesys design, and D answers an analytics question instead.

A targets question topics, drop-offs and quote starts with identity validation, consent and accountable reporting deliverables, B describes useful built-in engagement measures without a concrete quote or drop-off implementation, and C and D equally provide a cautious data route but focus on generic recommendations and purchases instead of the requested measures.

D maps all requested channels into schemas, ingestion, identity stitching and tested Workspace reports, C offers a sound generic connection and identity plan without the channel-specific ingestion design, B mainly implements Concierge and web reporting, and A largely describes capabilities without an implementation or shared-customer identity method.

A and D equally provide a complete scoped mirroring method with join checks, reconciliation and tested updates and deletes, B adds useful Snowflake access and privacy considerations but omits comparable validation, and C explains the core schema and synchronization approach with fewer accountable outputs and no effort or reconciliation commitment.

A addresses both directions with consented identity capture and a Salesforce API integration although its inbound CRM method remains thin, B and C equally detail only the Salesforce-to-CJA half with useful reconciliation, and D also misses outbound website and Concierge delivery while spending space on unrelated conversation review.

A explicitly includes BI extension permissions, limits and reconciled dashboards, D earns comparable credit with a signed Power BI specification, query design and separately estimated dashboard delivery, B supplies a solid similar plan without the explicit extension permission, and C offers the basic route and checks with fewer delivery commitments.

C connects the existing Marketo instance to website tracking and forms as well as CJA ingestion, identity and reconciliation, B covers the CJA side but leaves the website connection unspecified, and A and D equally concentrate on email setup and Munchkin while omitting the requested CJA integration.

B supplies relevant nonpublic-information classification and role design but leaves consent enforcement and activation controls unclear, C and D equally provide collection gating and withdrawal tests with thin storage and GLBA-specific safeguards, and A substitutes audience analytics for the requested privacy design.

C trains all three requested groups on their actual tasks with practical sign-off, recordings and role-specific guides, A and B provide equivalent author-only coverage despite different hour estimates, and D focuses on Coworker usage while largely missing Compliance, analyst and handover needs.

A combines permissions, tested reusable workflows, a pilot, training for all 35 marketers and funded ongoing adoption, C and D equally provide a useful pilot and handover while assuming setup and omitting broader rollout detail, and B commits mainly to defining two workflows.

D covers monthly website releases, monitoring, Concierge sampling and source regression checks but leaves the requested support hours and response times as an unresolved placeholder, B and C equally cover only conversation review, and A offers no operational service plan.

B defines a monthly prompt-maintenance, trend-reporting, prioritization and content-improvement service with quantified effort and sampling caveats, A and D equally offer content production without Brand Visibility reporting, and C explains measurement categories and bounded experience changes without a concrete monthly reporting service.

notes: Substantively equivalent answers received equal scores; opening quotations, formatting, answer position and isolated differences in estimated hours did not independently determine quality.

The strongest answers tied methods to Cedar Prairie constraints and supplied verifiable deliverables; many alternatives covered only one half of a requirement or substituted material from another topic.

Additional Workfront, Marketo Qualifier or CJA package requirements were assessed for explained relevance rather than treated as automatic errors; the Genesys bridge, approval enforcement and conditional Concierge data routes remain implementation uncertainties requiring validation.
Planning-hour estimates seldom became dated delivery commitments, and the unresolved support-hours placeholder materially weakened the most complete monthly operations answer.
All 96 answers were scored within the supplied word-limit determination, with no length penalties and no scoring of unpresented RFP requirements.
